questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨2z,\,x+y,\,y-z⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(2z-(x+y)+(y-z)) \\  & =\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{z-x}{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}{∬}_{S}z-x\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}y\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [x]_{0}^{3} \\  & =-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2{z}^{2}-x+2(y-{z}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{2y-x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2y-x}{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{S}2y-x\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=x+2y+1$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=\sqrt{2}.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+2y+1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-1.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+2y+1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z+5,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨x+2y+6,\,x-2y,\,3x-2y⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}((x+2y+6)+2(x-2y)-(3x-2y)) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(x+2y+6+2x-4y-3x+2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{6}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\sqrt{6}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
